title: Beef tacos with pico de gallo
skill: An even dice for pico de gallo

notes.text: Brown the beef in two batches, so it browns instead of steaming.

move.title: The dice is the dish
move.body: Pico de gallo is nothing but diced tomato, onion, and chile with cilantro, lime, and salt, so every cube shows. Today you'll dice it with a chef's knife, cube by even cube, then brown seasoned ground beef to 160°F for the tacos.

callback.body: If you made Baja fish tacos, you've diced pico before. This time you'll hold the knife the way chefs do and aim for cubes all the same size, about ¼ inch, because even cubes are the whole point of this unit.

why.title: The pinch grip
why.body: Pinch the blade just in front of the handle between your thumb and the side of your bent pointer finger, and wrap your other fingers around the handle. Holding the blade, not just the handle, gives you control of the tip, so each cut goes exactly where you aim it.

why.title: The claw
why.body: Your other hand holds the food with the fingertips curled under and the knuckles forward. The flat of the blade rests against your knuckles, which guide it. Your fingertips stay behind the edge, so the knife can't reach them.

why.title: Planks, sticks, cubes
why.body: Every dice works the same way. Cut flat planks, cut the planks into sticks, then cut across the sticks. If the planks and sticks are even, the cubes are too.

why.title: Scoop out the wet middle
why.body: The seeds in a tomato sit in watery jelly. Salt pulls that water out, so pico made with the seeds turns to soup. Scooped out first, the pico stays chunky.

why.title: Spoon off the fat
why.body: Ground beef gives off fat as it browns. Spooned off before the spices go in, it doesn't make the tacos greasy, and the spices coat the meat instead of floating in fat.

wrong.sign: The cubes are all different sizes
wrong.fix: Go back to even planks. Most uneven dice starts with uneven first cuts.

wrong.sign: The tomato squashes instead of cutting
wrong.fix: The knife is dull, or you're pressing down. Slide the blade forward through the skin as you cut, and hone the knife before you start.

wrong.sign: The onion falls apart while you cut it
wrong.fix: The root got cut off. Hold the layers together with your claw hand and cut slowly.

wrong.sign: The beef is gray and watery, not browned
wrong.fix: The pan was crowded or not hot enough. Turn the heat up and leave the beef alone for a minute between stirs.

quiz.q: In the claw, what guides the side of the knife?
quiz.explain: Fingertips stay curled back, behind the edge.

quiz.q: Why do you scoop the seeds out of the tomatoes?
choices: So the pico doesn't turn watery
quiz.explain: Salt pulls the water out of the seed jelly.

quiz.q: What temperature does ground beef need to reach?
quiz.explain: Grinding mixes surface bacteria all through the meat (Unit 1).

steps.text: Set the cutting board on a damp paper towel so it can't slide. Hold the chef's knife in a pinch grip.
steps.tip: Hone the knife first if it hasn't been honed today (this week's knowledge page).

steps.text: Cut each tomato into quarters from top to bottom. Scoop out the seeds and watery middle with the spoon.
Lay each quarter skin side down. Cut it into strips about ¼ inch wide, then line the strips up and cut across them into ¼-inch cubes. Put them in the medium bowl.
steps.look: Cubes about the size of a pea, all close to the same size.
steps.tip: Slide the blade forward through the skin instead of pressing down.

steps.text: Cut the onion in half from top to bottom, through the root, and peel it, leaving the root on. Lay each half flat side down. Holding it with the claw, cut strips ¼ inch apart from the top end toward the root, stopping just before the root.
Cut across the strips, ¼ inch apart, from the top end back toward the root, so cubes fall away. Throw away the root end. Add the onion to the bowl.
steps.look: Cubes about the size of the tomato cubes.

steps.text: If you're using the jalapeño, cut it in half the long way and scrape out the seeds and white ribs with the spoon. Cut it into thin strips, then dice it very fine. Add it to the bowl, and wash your hands right away.
steps.tip: Don't touch your eyes or face until you've washed your hands.

steps.text: Chop the cilantro fine and add it to the bowl with the lime juice and {qty:salt} salt. Stir, and let the pico sit while you cook the beef.
steps.tip: Salt pulls the flavor out as it sits. Taste it again before serving.

steps.text: Heat the oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers.
Crumble the beef into the pan in pieces, straight from the package.
Throw away the package and wash your hands with soap.
Cook the beef, breaking it into small crumbles with the wooden spoon, until it's browned with no pink left.
steps.tip: Leave it alone for a minute between stirs so it browns.

steps.text: Push the beef into a pile and slide the thermometer into the middle. It needs to read at least 160°F. If it doesn't, cook 1 more minute and check again.
Tip the pan a little and spoon the fat into the heatproof bowl. Let it cool, then throw it away in the trash, not down the sink.
Add the chili powder, cumin, garlic powder, oregano, the beef's salt, and the water. Stir and simmer until the liquid has cooked down and coats the beef. Turn off the stove.
Stack the tortillas, wrap them in a damp paper towel, and microwave until warm and soft. Keep them wrapped in the kitchen towel.
Fill each tortilla with beef and a spoonful of pico, and cheese and sour cream if you're using them.
steps.tip: Use two tortillas stacked together if they tear.
